abstract: |
 The length- and age-structure of commercial landings is a crucial input to fish stock assessment. In the Northeast United States, NOAA Fisheries deploys samplers to fish dealers to measure the length of commercially landed fish.  When there are few or no samples of a market category of fish, the informational content of fish prices can be used to make an inference about the size of an unsampled market category. We use the Black Sea Bass fishery in the Northeast United States to illustrate our approach to using economic data to inform stock assessments.  There are 5 common market categories: Jumbo, Large, Medium, Small, and Unclassified.  From 2020 to 2023, 5 to 10% of commercial landings were in the “Unclassified” market category but no fish in this category were measured. A preliminary hedonic model confirms that prices vary by market category: “Unclassified” Black Sea Bass are priced between “Large” and “Medium” fish. We fit a categorical Random Forest to predict the probability that a transaction belongs to a particular market category using prices and other variables.  We use the results to predict the probability of the “Unclassified” belonging to any of the other market categories, allowing us to construct a price-informed length structure of commercial landings.

# Introduction

<!--- Include the next 2 child documents.   --->
```{r, child=here("writing", c("summary.Rmd")),  eval=FALSE}
```

The age-structure of commercial landings is a crucial input to the quantitative 
stock assessments in the Northeast United States. In the Northeast US, commercial
fishing vessels catch fish and sell their landed fish to dealers who sort
the catch into market categories.   The National Marine Fisheries Service
deploys biological samplers to measure the length of commercially landed fish. 
Otoliths are collected and aged from a subset of measured fish. That data are used
to build spatiotemporally explicit age-length keys that convert the landed weight of all market categories into numbers-at-age
of commercial landings. The stock assessment enterprise in the Northeast U.S. has a series of business 
rules for handling gaps in the market category to age relationship that arise 
when certain market categories are either not sampled or under-sampled. This 
typically involves borrowing from neighboring strata, seasons, or years.

In this article, we propose an approach that uses the price of fish 
to fill this data gap. We apply this approach to the stock assessment for black sea bass (*Centropristis striata*) in the Northeast United States. Dealers purchase black sea bass from fishing vessels and sort them into in market categories. From 2020 to 2023, 5 to 10% of
commercial landings were in the “Unclassified” market category; however no fish in this category were measured. 

The general approach is as follows.  As part of our exploratory data analysis, we estimate a simple hedonic model to confirm that prices vary by market category. We tune, train, and validate a random forest model to classify fish into one of the four primary market categories. Finally, we conduct out-of-sample prediction on Unclassified fish.

Our ultimate goal is to improve the stock assessment enterprise by including more 
information about the true size of un-measured "Unclassified" fish. This requires 
predictions of the Unclassified fish to be aggregated to the year-stock unit level and the accuracy of
an individual prediction is of no interest. This method is good because it can be applied to existing streams of historical data and can be used to reconfigure sampling coverage.

# Background

```

## Catching, Classifying, and Selling  Fish

Black sea bass are caught by fishing vessels that typically use bottom trawl and
pot/trap gear; gillnets and hook-and-line are less commonly used. Firms can target both
sizes of fish and their catch of other species, but cannot perfectly control 
what they catch and land.  The ability to target, and therefore the landings composition,
is impacted by fishing regulations, which vary by state. For example, the seasonal inshore movement during 
the spring and offshore movement  during the fall [@Moser2009] can affect the composition of landings.  When fish are offshore, they are
less available to smaller vessels or those that are registered in states that 
manage with stringent possession limits.  Strong year classes can make a size 
class temporarily more available during certain years.


The fishery is jointly managed by the ASFMC and the MAFMC. Regulations are enacted 
by GARFO.  From 1996 through 2003, the fishery was managed primarily by quarterly catch 
limits for the entire fishery. There were early closures in 1999 (Quarters 2,3,4),
2000 (2,3,4), and 2001 (all). Quota was allocated to each state staring in 2003
(Amendment 13) and is monitored based on landed state. In 2021, the formula 
that allocates commercial quotas to the states was revised; 75% of the quota is
allocated according to historical  fishing and 25% is allocated in proportion 
to where the biomass is located.

There is some catch that occurs within state waters by fishing vessels that do not 
have federal permits. Three states  (MD, DE, and VA) 
have IFQ programs that started in 2004. Current minimum size limits are 11" 
or 12".  Possession limits vary widely by state; the IFQ states do not have 
possession limits while Massachusetts and Rhode Island use seasonally varying 
limits that have been as strict as 50 lbs/day or as loose as 1,500 lbs per week.


```{r length-histograms,echo=FALSE,out.width="48%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Length and Real (2023Q1 USD) Price Frequencies by market categories, 2013-2024."}
knitr::include_graphics(c(here("images","background","LenFq.Mktcomb.pdf"),here("images","exploratory","wprice_histograms_vertical_NR.pdf")))
```


Fishing vessels catch fish and deliver it to buyers (fish dealer) who classify the fish into market categories and pay the vessel.  This market structure, in which the quantity and quality supplied is determined before prices adjust to equalize quantity supplied and quantity demanded, is common in fish markets [@Barten1989; @Kristofersson2007;@Gobillon2017].  There are four prevalent market categories (Jumbo, Large, Medium/Market, and Small), plus an "Unclassified" category^[Following the stock assessment, "Mixed or Unsized" is aggregated with "Unclassified";  "Extra Small" and "PeeWee" are aggregated with Small category; "Extra Large" is aggregated with "Jumbo"].  Figure \@ref(fig:length-histograms) illustrates that fish in the "Unclassified" or "Mixed" category are precisely that, an unobserved combination of the other market categories. No standardized definition of the market categories exists and the definitions themselves may vary over time (year-to-year, month-to-month) and geography (state-to-state or stock area to stock area).  Many fish dealers act just as wholesalers, simply selling whole fish to processors, restaurants, or final consumers. Other fish dealers are vertically integrated with some downstream entities, processing and selling filleted fish to downstream customers. Integration of the harvest and wholesale/dealer activities also occurs.

The market categories exist because downstream buyers care about the sizes of fish; prices of most types of fish depend on the size of fish. Prices are also influenced by other attributes, including freshness, fat content, water content, buyer- and seller- effects, and the quantity attributes supplied to the market^[@McConnell2000, @Carroll2001, @Kristofersson2004, @Kristofersson2007,  @Lee2014, @Hammarlund2015,  @Gobillon2017, and @Ardini2018 are just a few examples.]. 

Prices can be used to predict market category only if prices actually vary by market category. Figure  \@ref(fig:length-histograms) suggests that is the case and a simple hedonic model verifies that prices do indeed vary by market category (Table \ref{HedonicMarketCats}) .  The price of Jumbo black sea bass is approximately \$6 per pound, while the price of medium black sea bass is closer to \$3.70.  Interestingly, the Unclassified market category has an average price of \$4.26 per pound, in between that of Large and Medium fish, suggesting that Unclassified fish may be a mix of these other two categories^[A hedonic price model is not the main focus of this research, nevertheless, we report more details about the simple model in the Appendix.].


\input{../results/hedonic_table_market_cats.tex}


The model is fit by ordinary least squares. In addition to the presented coefficients, the model contains controls for gear, landed state, year, month, daily landings and daily landings$^2$.  All but the final two terms are factor variables that are "one-hot" encoded. 

## Black Sea Bass and the Stock Assessment Enterprise 

### Stock assessment 


Black sea bass are protogynous hermaphrodites, reach maturity around 2-3 years old, live approximately 8-12 years, and change sex from female to male in older, larger ages.
They exhibit seasonal movement patterns, overwintering offshore in the fall and winter in deeper waters but returning to inshore waters in early spring to spawn. They prefer to
aggregate in structured habitats and are caught near reefs and wrecks. Though black sea bass north of Cape Hatteras are managed as a single stock, a distinction is drawn around Hudson Canyon that subdivides this stock into a northern and southern subunit with assumed, though minimal, movement between these groups which has been confirmed through tagging studies [@Moser2008].

Before 2023, reference point calculations for black sea bass had been taken from two Age Structured Assessment Program (ASAP) models, north or south of Hudson Canyon. Since 2023, the black sea bass stock assessment model has been a single age-based Woods Hole Assessment Model (WHAM) with movement assumed and estimated between the northern and southern subregions, albeit with a strong prior derived from a priori tagging data [@Miller2025]. Each subunit has distinct assumed life history input like weight at age, length-weight relationships, and maturity at age. The assessment model also estimates distinct parameters for each subunit including abundance, recruitment, fishing mortality, and selectivity. Because the recruitment is distinct, the subunits can have noticeably different size compositions, and the northern subunit had large age classes in 2012 and 2018. 

The assessment model is fit to catch data from the commercial and recreational fishery, and two sources of fisheries-independent indices: model-based indices from a VAST model [@Thorson2019; @Hansell2026] and recreational catch-per-angler indices. The conversion from raw catch data to catch-at-age necessitates using portside and observer sampling data of lengths and ages (via otoliths). Because such data can be highly spatiotemporally dependent, these data are aggregated to the year, semester (Jan-Jun or Jul-Aug), and region (north or south).

### Port Sampling for Ages and Lengths 

A port sampling program has existed in the northeast United States for more than three decades,
collecting vital biological data like lengths, weights, ages, and stomach samples that directly support
the fisheries stock assessment process.

Throughout its history, the program has been staffed by federal port agents or contracted companies, and funded by the National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS).
Because staffing and financial resources are limited, sampling priorities been rigidly set through a two-stage  prioritization system.  In the first stage, stocks 
with analytical assessments, high average recent landings, and high profiles are allocated more samples.  In the second stage, the stock assessment lead uses their knowledge of the fishery and assessment to request samples from particular regions, times of year, and market categories.  These decisions heavily influenced by availability of historical data, timing and location of
commercial landings, spatio-temporal abundance of the stock, and stock assessment model.

Though the number of collected lengths across the entire
program exceeded 200,000 annually between 2015-2019 with 7 full-time port samplers, in 2024 less than 50,000 lengths were collected by 3 full-time and 3 part-time samplers.
Efforts have been supplemented by the MAFMC and Massachusetts DMF but with falling funding sources and rising costs per sample, the amount of these critical biological data 
is well below what it was ten years ago. A recent merger of the portside sampling program with the NEFSC observer program is anticipated to increase efficiency and sampling. 

Biosamplers try to meet the sample requests by efficiently targeting ports at times where a variety of species and sized fish are likely to be landed. Often they
may specifically target a port known to land a specific or obscure market category to fulfill the scientific requests. These requests may go unfulfilled, causing data gaps. When data gaps exist, stock assessment modelers will relax the specificity of the information, i.e., borrow across regions or semesters, and in
extreme cases may take length and age distribution data from fisheries-independent sources rather than from the catch subsamples. However, it is preferable to have unbiased and precise
sample information to convert the total landings in pounds to landings-at-age, which are the necessary format to run age-based stock assessments like in ASAP or WHAM.


```{r LenHist2,echo=FALSE,out.width="32%", fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Length Frequencies by market categories, 2009-2024."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("images","background",c("LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2009-2013.png","LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2014-2018.png", "LenFq.Mktcomb.Region.Color.2019-2024.png") ))
```

Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) illustrates these data gaps and their attendant problems; there are no biosamples for Unclassified fish in the South region after 2013 and very few in the north, particularly after 2018^[All measured Unclassified fish in the 2019-2024 time period came from a 2 week time period in a single port in 2020.  There are also relatively few samples of Jumbo in the South from 2014-2018 and Small in the North from 2019-2024.].  In all three time periods, landed fish tend to be slightly smaller in the South region relative to the North region, reflecting differing regional tendencies for grading.  Filling data gaps in the South with data from the North is therefore likely to produce catch-at-length estimates that are too large. Within a region, borrowing data from a bordering market category is also likely to produce poor estimates of catch-at-length.  Borrowing data from adjacent time periods also may be problematic from both theoretical and empirical perspectives. Unclassified black sea bass must be allocated to an age category in order to conduct an age-structured stock assessment, but without any additional information Figure \@ref(fig:LenHist2) leaves the stock assessment scientists in an uncomfortable place. 



# Methods and Data

The goal of this research is to employ the economic information contained in prices to leave that uncomfortable place.  Because the stock assessment inputs our aggregated at the year-, semester-, and region, our goal is to generate accurate prediction of the true market category of the unclassified fish at that level. Neither the accuracy of an individual prediction nor the causal mechanisms by which one factor affects market category is of interest.  Machine learning approaches, which focus on accurate prediction of an outcome variable instead of the causal relationship between predictors and outcome, are attractive methods [@Varian2014; @Mullainathan2017; @Athey2019].  These approaches have proliferated in fisheries, ecology, and economics [@Rubbens2023; @Kuhn2024; @Akselrud2024]. Applications include from classifying fishing activity with Vessel Monitoring Systems or Autotmatic Identification Systems [@Russo2011], building predictive models of fishing vessel trip costs [@Chan2021] and prices [@francca2024price], and image processing [@Alvarez-Ellacuria2020].

## Modeling Probability of Class Membership with a Random Forest

In this application, we use a multinomial random forest model [@Breiman2001; @Malley2012] to model the probability that a transaction is in one of the four principle market categories^[Random forest pplications of these models in fisheries include classification of acoustic data [@Fallon2016, @Proud2020], fishery metiers [@Oostdijk2024], and habitat [@Liu2025].].  Random Forests are can viewed as ensembles of Classification and Regression Trees [CART, @Breiman1984].  A classification tree repeatedly partitions observations into two groups based on a single explanatory variable.  The optimal explanatory variable to use and partitioning value is selected by minimizing a measure of variation among member of the partition; we use gini impurity.  Intuitively, the optimal split produces groups with homogenous outcomes.  The CART algorithm grows tress by continuing to split until all nodes are homogenous or a user-specified early stopping criteria is met. 

Single classification trees are prone to poor out of sample performance; a tree grown to pure nodes is perfectly fit to the training dataset.  Random forests improve out of sample prediction by bootstrapping and restricting each bootstrap replication to a small number of randomly selected predictors [@Breiman2001; @Strobl2009; @Hastie2023 ].  Both modifications induce variation in the individual classification trees.  @Malley2012 and @Kruppa2014 average over the final nodes of random trees to assign probability of class membership, we adopt this approach. 

Like many machine learning models, random forests have hyperparameters which must be exogenously supplied. Results can be sensitive to these choices; models are typically tuned by searching for an optimal set of parameters using a subset of data and the selected parameters are validate model on a holdout sample.  Averaging methods, including Random forest models, are also known to be underconfident; high probabilities are understimated and low probabilities are overestimated.  This occurs because the model averaging process in which individual trees are aggregated into random forests averages away extreme values.  Calibration through an auxiliary model, is often necessary after fitting a random forest [@Niculescu-Mizil2005; @Kull2017; @Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024; @Ferrer2025].

To address these blah, we do a bunch of good stuff.  We split our dataset three ways; we use 70% of our dataset to tune the model hyperparameters, 15% to calibrate probabilities, and 15% to validate the model.  Simulation studies by [@Barreada2024] suggest tuning over the minimum node size (*min.n*) when using random forests in probability models. The number of randomly selected predictors (*mtry*) was also tuned over. We tune over two hyperparameters by performing a 10-fold cross validation study in which we grid search over the reasonable starting values of the two parameters.  We supplement the initial grid search by performing the bayesian tuning described by @Shahriari2016. Our cross-validation was stratified by market category to ensure that the proportion of each class in the folds approximately matched the initial compositions. We selected the optimal pair of hyperparameters that had the smallest log loss criterion function averaged over the ten folds. For each fold, log loss is computed as: 

\begin{equation}
\label{logloss1}
LogLoss = - \sum_{i=i}^N Y_{ik} ln(Pr_{ik})
\end{equation}
where $i$ indexes observations, $k$ indexes classes, $Y_{ik}=1$ if observation $i$ is a member of class $k$, and $Pr_{ik}$ is the predicted probability that observation $i$ is a member of class $k$.

After selecting the best hyperparamters, we refit the model on the entire 70% tuning dataset.  We use the fitted model to predict class membership for the 15% calibration sample. We visually assess whether the model is well-calibrated using commonly used calibration plots [@Ojeda2023; @Barreada2024]. We also use the Relative Calibration loss methods described in [@Ferrer2025] to assess whether calibration is necessary (it is) and to select among isotonic, beta, and multinomial calibration methods.

We apply the the trained model and the probability calibration routine to the final 15% of our data as a final validation.  We report adjusted fit metrics.  The random forest model is fit in R using the ``ranger`` package; we use  ``tidymodels`` packages to facilitate tuning, training, and out-of-sample predicting.  

After fitting the data, we predict out of sample on the Unclassified Landings.  We do this with  "soft probabilities", 
using the trained model to predict the probability of class memembership^[The alternative is to assign class membership to the highest predicted class] and then aggregating the 
landed pounds to the year-, market category-, and subregion level. 



## A Stylized Theoretical Model Guidances Our Modeling Approach 

The core concept of this research is simple: we can use the information contained in transaction level prices to infer something about the size of the Unclassified fish.  A simple theoretical model sketch can provide guidance about explanatory factors that belong in the model.  We start by assuming a single, perfectly-competitive market for *ex-vessel* fish in which there are many dealers and vessels, no vertical integration, no market power, no transactions costs, and  complete information.  Complete information implies that all buyers and sellers know everything there is to know, including all quality attributes of every lot of fish. No transactions costs means that sales are costless.  Under these conditions, the market prices encapsulate all relevant information.  <!--- We also assume there is no vertical integration between dealers and vessels: a dealer and a fishing vessel is not owned by the same firm and there is no "forward" contracting in which buyers and sellers agree in advance on a price. --->

To build intuition, we assume that, with the exception of market category, all fish are identical.  There three categories of fish: Jumbo, Large, and Unclassified. Prices of fish are constant and dealers strictly prefer Jumbo to Large, so the price of Jumbo is strictly greater than the price of Large: $p^J > p^L$.  The unclassified category is assumed to be a composite, and each transaction $i$ containing of $\alpha_i$ Jumbo and $(1-\alpha_i)$ Large. Because the buyers and sellers can observe this mix, the price of an unclassified transaction is:

\begin{equation}
\label{unknown1}
p_i= \alpha_i p^J+ (1-\alpha_i) p^L \hspace{2mm} \forall \hspace{2mm} \alpha \in [0,1]
\end{equation},

For any price between $p^L$ and $p^J$, we can perfectly deduce the underlying composition of the Unclassified transaction. This stylized fact drives us to use a model of probability of class membership for a transaction, as opposed to class membership. 

<!---We assume that dealers have a perfectly elastic demand curve for the two categories of fish, Jumbo and Large, and that they prefer Jumbo relative to large.  A perfectly elastic demand curve means that dealers will buy all Jumbo landings as long as the price of Jumbo is less than or equal to $p_J$. The same holds true for the Large market category. --->

Constant prices for each category is unrealistic for many reasons. In this application, sales transactions are of similar, but not identical goods.  The hedonic model (Table \ref{HedonicTableA}) suggests that many attributes, including size, method of production, and time of year impact prices.  There are many reasons this can occur.  Meat quality can vary within a season, resulting in different prices within a year.  Regional differences in transportation costs, processing costs,  or final consumer preferences and incomes can produce in regional variation in prices [@samuelson1954transfer; @Krugman1991a].  The demand curve for nearly fish is downward sloping: increases in quantity supplied of fish will reduce prices [@Lee2014; @Ardini2018, and Table \ref{HedonicTableA}].

Because many attributes impact prices, transactions of different size classes may have similar prices.  This suggests that attributes that are important in determining the price of fish should enter as factors in the machine learning model. Intuition for this can be seen in the following example based on the Table \ref{HedonicTableA}. Most fish are delivered "Round," dead with the gut in.  Some fish are delivered live, these receive a premium of approximately \$0.16 per pound. The mean price of a Small Live black sea bass is \$3.69 (=\$3.526 +\$0.164), which is very close to the mean price of Medium Round \$3.75.  Without including an indicator for Live, a machine learning model would be likely to classify "Small Live" black sea bass as "Medium."  We collect all factors that impact prices, except market category, into $Z_i$.  

\begin{equation}
\label{demand}
p_i = f(c_i, Z_i),
\end{equation}


### More that two market categories

When there are more than two market categories (say, Medium), equation \ref{unknown1} becomes:

\begin{align}
p&= \beta_1 p^J+ \beta_2 p^L + (1-\beta_1-\beta_2) \\\label{unknown2}
\sum_{i=1}^3 \beta_i&=1\\
\geq 0 & \beta_i \geq 1 \hspace{2mm} \forall i=1,2
\end{align}
Intuitively, observing a transaction price that falls between two market categories does not imply that a transaction is a linear combination of the two adjacent categories. This suggests that including other proxies for beyond just prices and factors that affect prices is necessary.

### The Competitive Market Equilibrium and the Law of One Price

The assumption of a competitive market is critical to our ability to use prices to infer market category. Law of One Price. It ensures that the prices capture all relevant quality information and that there is a single price^[All identical goods will sell at the same price; observations of identical goods with different prices suggest that some conditions of a competitive market are absent [@Lamont2003].  Variations of the law of one price that account for heterogenous goods, informational assymmetries [@Salop1982], and different data availability have been proposed and tested statistically [@Asche1999; @Nielsen2009; @Pettersen2018].].  If a dealer offered a lower price for Jumbo than the prevailing price, a competitive market ensures that this dealer would not purchase any Jumbo fish.  Vessels with Jumbo fish would simply sell to another dealer.  Conversely, if a dealer offered a higher price for Jumbo than the prevailing price, then that dealer would purchase all the Jumbo fish and this new "too high" price would become the new prevailing price. Presumably, the dealer would want this situation.

A perfectly competatve market is unlikely, but the law of one price suggests a few things. We should not expect the law of one price to hold perfectly and unconditionally, but in imperfectly and conditionally. That is, all black sea bass does not trade at the same price; however, black sea bass with similar attributes will trade at similar prices.  Therefore the classification model should include variables explain prices in the classification model. These include attributes like gear used, whether the fish is sold live, state of landing, daily quantity landed, and time period of landing.  We should expect the prices of similar goods to be more similar than prices of different goods, although a working definition of similar can be tricky.  In particular, instead of adding prices to the random forest model directly, we use prices to construct a distance metrics between the transaction and "typical" price of each market category.  This follows the suggestion from @Mullainathan2017 to use insights from  economic theory to guide a machine learning model's search for underlying structure. 

Outside the DGP, we should remove them from the training dataset and refrain from predicting class membership for those those types of observations.  Intuitively, if the price does not convey any information about sizes, then we should not try to infer anything from prices. We can think of three scenarios where this is likely to occur.  

First, there is less quality assurance and quality control for the species value field which we use to construct prices. While there are checks to ensure that the values are within a reasonable range, firms that do not report accurately may not be required to improve their reporting accuracy. We handle this by excluding transactions with prices that are too high (over \$15 per pound) or too low (under \$0.15 per pound).  Second, buyers and sellers may be owned by the same entity, making definition of the  *ex-vessel* prices insensitive to market forces.  Fully disentangling ownership is difficult, but inspection of the data suggested that some dealers-vessel pairs were exclusively trading with each other, suggesting some vertical integration.  Third, firms may also participate in forward contracting in which the price of fish is determined well in advance of landing.  To account  for the final two, we excluded transactions from dealer-year-market category combinations where the standard deviation of prices was less than 0.10.  Table Summary statistics describes characteristics of the full dataset and the cleaned dataset.

## Data

Economic theory and on-the-ground subject-matter expertise (the black sea bass stock assessment and commercial fishery) guide selection of explanatory factors and factor engineering [@Mullainathan2017]. 

The buyers (dealers) are the entities that classify the fish and dealers are likely to have an unobserved propensity to 
grade fish into particular classes. This unobserved heterogeneity poses two challenges.  

Traditional estimators often use a full set of binary indicator variables to account for individual-specific 
effects; doing so in Random Forests can lead to both overfitting
[@Breiman2001; @Hastie2023] and bias [c.f @Strobl2007; @Strobl2009]. 
Instead we use a variation of target encoding.  Application of a standard
target-encoding system would involve computing dealer-specific class probabilities
over the 2015-2025 time period and including those probabilities as factors. This feels 
somewhat troubling to an economist concerned about simultaneity, a concern which
may be misplaced. Nevertheless, we compute annual dealer-specific class probabilities
and enter these, with a 1 year lag, as predictors instead. Dealers 
that did not buy or sell black sea bass in the previous year time have missing values.


This is pretty rough notation
\begin{equation}
\label{dealer_specific}
D_{cjy} = \frac{\sum_{t \in y} lndlb_{jt}} {\sum_c \sum_{t\in y} lndlb_{jt}}
\end{equation}

Second, @Roberts2017 note that standard cross-validation techniques can be overly optimistic
when observations are dependent but are implicitly treated as independent during a random cross-validation.   This occurs because 
the hold out data used for cross-validation is not actually independent. @Roberts2017 suggest
that the practical implications of this depend on the purposes of the model; if prediction on 
"similar" data is the goal, then a standard cross-validation may be appropriate.
We try two methods of cross validation in our training.  The first is the standard random cross-validation; observations are assigned randomly into folds.  In the second method, we group by "dealer identifier" so that all of a dealer's observations are contained
in either the training dataset or the validation dataset.  This ensures that the
validation fold does not inadvertently contain "training data", which would lead
to overly optimistic model fit.  Keeping the entirety of dealer's
observations in either the training or validation datasets reduces the likelihood
of information leakage^[Information leakage occurs when a model essentially 
memorizes the input data, leading to validation metrics that are overly-optimistic.  
This can cause poor out of sample predictions.]

We use CAMS data from 2015 to 2024 to train our data. The CAMS data complied by GARFO consists of dealer transactions matched to vessel trip reports. We briefly describe this datasource.  Dealer data are transaction-level reports of fish purchases by federally permitted fish dealers from each vessel.  They are disaggregated to the trip and market category level and include landed weight (pounds) and value (nominal US Dollars).  Prices are converted to Real 2023Q1 values using the CPI for all urban consumers (CPIAUCSL). Vessel trip report data arereports of fishing activity by federally permitted vessels that are disaggregated to the statistical area-gear-trip level and include information about area fished, gear used, trip length, and estimates of quantity kept (hail weights) and discarded at the species level.   Matching is performed based on the Vessel trip report serial number. When this match fails, matching is done based on the vessel permit number, dealer identifier, and date which are contained in both the vessel reports and the dealer reports.  When vessels fish in multiple statistical areas or using multiple gears, they file more than one report per trip.  One of the functions of the CAMS data system is to allocate trip-level dealer records to the appropriate statistical area.  CAMS allocates in proportion to the hail weights on those trip reports, splitting a single trip record into multiple observations.

Black Sea Bass may be caught by firms without a federal fishing permit and sold to dealers without a federal dealer permit.  In some states, firms without a federal permit can fish for black sea bass in state waters (within 3 miles of land) and sell it to fish dealers who do not have a federal permit.  These sales are also in our data and the CAMS system imputes both statistical area (area adjacent to landing port) and gear used when missing. 

Our observational units are sales transactions; the dependent variable is the market category and explanatory variables include transformations of price and other variables that impact prices.  In our exploratory analysis (the hedonic model presented in Table \ref{HedonicTableA}) and our Random Forest, we frequency weight the observations by the landed weight in pounds^[We use pounds, instead of kilograms, because the data are reported in integer pounds, and frequency weighting requires integers].  This treats our observations as if they were repeated observations of the sale of a pound of fish.  We do this for a few reasons.  First, they are exactly that.  Second, our goal is to obtain an aggregate weight prediction of the underlying unobserved market category of Unclassified fish; we are not interested in predictions of aggregate transactions.  Frequency weighting affects our methods in a few ways. We use log-loss as the criterion function for tuning and calibration; the log-loss function is modified to weight each observation by pounds. During the fitting of the individual trees, observations are drawn with replacement in proportion to their freqency weight. This results in bootstrap datasets which more closely resemble the frequency weighted data (instead of the unweighted data).  We attempted to calibrate using weighted data without success and we discuss reasons and paths forward in the discussion section.

source(here("R_code","analysis", "fit_random_forest","BSB.Classification.Recipe.R"))

```


Machine learning algorithms can often benefit from preprocessing of data. Missing values for predictors are handled by splitting the data as if they didn't exist, assigning the observations with missing values to each nodes, and selecting the node that has the greatest decrease in impurity.  We treat factors variables as "unordered" and follow the implementation method described in @Hastie2009.  We grow 500 trees when tuning the model and when training the final model.

# Results

Our procedure is to tune two hyperaparameters using 75\% of our dataset, calibrate on 15\%, and validate on the final 15\% holdout sample. We present results of the initial tuning, calibration, and validation.  To summarize, the initial tuning found optimal hyperparameter values of $mtry=19$ and $min_n=66$ respectively.  The calibration steps find moderate gain from isotonic calibration, and the validation shows the model fits well. 

## Tuning and Calibration results


```{r rocTune,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="ROC curves from tuning"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","tune", glue("roc_tune_nocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf")))
```

In-sample ROC curves from tuning are quite similar across folds
and the initial steepness indicates the tuned random forest is good (Figure  \@ref(fig:rocTune)).

```{r vip,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Variable importance measured as mean decrease in accuracy from permutation of each predictor. Top 20 of predictors shown"}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","final", glue("vipnocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf")))
```

The VIP confirms that prices are very important in predicting market category (Figure  \@ref(fig:vip)).

The calibration step \@ref(fig:calibrationplots) illustrates an issue that commonly affects predictions of Random Forest models. A well calibrated model will be close to the 45 degree line.  For three of the four classes, the aggregation of individual trees leads to underconfidence; observations with high predicted probabilities have even higher true probabilities. The exception is the Small market category; this may be indicative of class imbalance in the dataset.  The isotonic regression used to calibrate predictions corrects much, but not all, of the model underconfidence and improves the log loss (Equation \ref{logloss1}) by approximately 5\% (from 0.526 to 0.497).  

```{r calibrationplots,echo=FALSE,fig.show='hold', fig.align='center',fig.cap="Plots of true event rates versus predicted event rates for raw (left panel) and calibrated predictions (right panel).  We use an Isotonic regression to calibrate."}
knitr::include_graphics(here("results","ranger","final", c(glue("cal_windowed_nocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf"),glue("cal_isovalidate_windownocluster{pred_vintage}.pdf") ) ) )
```

# Discussion

A reasonable method for filling in gaps in historical data.

Could be used for other species. 

Principal-Agent problem in collecting samples. Contracting firm is paid by sample, firms try to maximize profits and individuals try to maximize utility. Collecting samples from "easy" locations is, by definition, easier and more profitable than meeting difficult requests.

Investigate how to combine existing biosampling data with these pricing information (complement instead of substitute).

Could we use this to go directly to sizes? 

The RF calibration didn't work so well with weighted observations.
  - isotonic has so many ties. And the weighting produces very 'lumpy' points.

Our RF model does very well at predicting observations and comparatively worse at weights. Why?

Our loss function is very simple for tuning is very simple. But our data is not, it's 'ordered'.  Predicting a true Jumbo to be a Large is better than predicting it to be a Medium.
